scenes.title: Where and when
narration: The passacaglia originated in early 17th-century Spain as a strummed guitar interlude between songs or dances, taking its name from 'pasar' (to pass) and 'calle' (street).
The first written musical examples emerged in Italy in 1606.
Girolamo Frescobaldi redefined it in the late 1620s into continuous variations over a bass ostinato.

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Historically used for theatrical interludes and religious processions.
In contemporary South America, it marks civic holidays, national anniversaries, and town honors (such as the pasacalles written for Ecuadorian cities).
In the Basque Country, the kalejira serves a vital social function, allowing community members to display and strengthen social integration through collective street movement.

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: In European baroque contexts, it was performed as a slow, gravetier court dance in triple metre.
In South America, particularly Chile and Ecuador, it functions as a processional or street-band dance performed during civic holidays and town festivals.
In the Basque Country, the kalejira variant involves participants moving through streets in human chains, occasionally stopping to dance fandangos and arin-arins.

scenes.title: Listen
narration: Characterized primarily by a basso ostinato—a recurring melodic bass line (usually 4, 6, or 8 bars long) that serves as a harmonic anchor while upper voices vary freely.
European baroque iterations are typically in a minor key and written in triple metre (3/4), whereas 19th-century Andean adaptations often use a binary rhythm (2/4) resembling a march.
Listen for the guitar, lute, baroque guitar, organ.
The pulse is 3/4 (European Baroque) or 2/4 (Andean South American) at about 106 beats a minute.

A solemn, steady foundational bass pattern anchors fluctuating upper melodies, shifting from the contemplative minor-key gravity of Baroque organ and strings to the bright, brassy, and nostalgic syncopation of Andean street bands.

scenes.title: The people
narration: Girolamo Frescobaldi, Johann Sebastian Bach, François Couperin, Louis Couperin, George Frideric Handel, Dietrich Buxtehude, Johannes Brahms, Anton Webern, Benjamin Britten, and Dmitri Shostakovich.

Variants include the European baroque passacaille/passacaglia, the Chilean instrumental brass-band pasacalle, Colombian street-band music, Ecuadorian city pasacalles (such as 'El chulla quiteño'), Peruvian festive street estampas, and the Basque kalejira.

Derived from early 17th-century Spanish guitar street interludes; branched into the European baroque variation form (closely intertwined with the chaconne) and the South American Andean march and civic song tradition.
